chapter_theme: The impermanence of the body (யாக்கை நிலையாமை): the body is a clay pot, a thatched hut, a walled temple that falls apart; when the life that dwelt in it leaves, kin weep, burn it, bathe and forget, and only vows and knowledge go with the dead.
structure_note: Two kinds of verse alternate: scenes of a death and its funeral (145, 147, 148, 150, 151, 153, 155, 157, 162), and images of the body as a made thing, pot or hut or temple, often in riddling numbers (143, 146, 154, 158, 159, 161). 165 and 166 turn to what follows death, and 167 closes on the dancer who has left the skin bag.

143.reading: From one clay come two kinds of vessel, one that stays firm and one bound up with bad deeds; as the unfired returns to clay when rain falls from the sky, so people die past counting.
143.nuance: The two vessels are most simply the fired and the unfired pot; line 2 (திண்ணென்று இருந்தது தீவினைச் சேர்ந்தது) can also mean that what seemed firm was itself joined to bad deeds, so that no body is truly fired. எண்ணின்றி may be 'without number' or 'without their thinking of it'.

144.reading: When the roof that held one's goods falls, worn with use, the women and children who ate from it do not follow; nothing goes along the road with the dead but the vows they kept and the knowledge they gained.
144.nuance: The roof (கூரை) is the body, as in 146 and 161. விரதம் (vow, observance) and ஞானம் are the only companions named, not wealth or kin.

145.reading: The whole town gathers and wails aloud, takes away his name and calls him a corpse, carries him to the thorny burning ground and burns him, then bathes in water and stops thinking of him.
145.nuance: The name is removed before the body: பேரினை நீக்கிப் பிணமென்று பேரிட்டு. The last act is not the burning but the forgetting (நினைப்பொழிந்தார்) that the bath completes.

146.reading: There are two posts, one ridge beam and thirty-two great rafters in the frame; the roof above comes apart, and once it has, the life cannot enter it again as before.
146.nuance: The hut is the body: the two posts are the legs and the ridge beam is commonly taken as the spine. What the thirty-two rafters (பருங்கழி) stand for is not fixed; the ribs or the teeth are the usual guesses.

147.reading: Sickness ripened, the deeds that were done ran out, the body came apart and its frame rotted; they put a hand to the nose, covered him, carried him off and set out an offering for the crows.
147.nuance: சீக்கை and அலகு are unclear: சீக்கை is read as sickness or phlegm, அலகு as the beam of the frame. Death follows when the store of past deeds is used up (செய்வினை மூட்டிற்ற). The hand at the nose tests for breath; the crows' offering is the rice set out at the rites, or the body itself left to crows.

148.reading: He had food cooked and ate it, talked privately with his tender wife, said his left side ached a little, lay down, and lay there gone.
148.nuance: The verse is a row of ordinary verbs ending in கிடந்தொழிந்தாரே, so that the death arrives as one more act of the day. இறை here means 'a little', not 'the Lord'.

149.reading: In the public square the man raised a mansion, in the square he gained a palanquin and rode in it, in the square he gave away three crores; when the cry came that he had gone, he did not turn back.
149.nuance: மன்றத்தே repeats three times: a whole public life of building, honour and giving. The palanquin may be a mark of honour, or, as in 153, the bier he rides at last. சென்றத்தா என்ன is unclear; it may be the mourners' cry 'he has gone, father'.

150.reading: With sweet talk they marry and live with that husband till their love is sated and they stop thinking of him; then they lay him on the bier, weep as is fitting, burn the bond in fire and make the offering.
150.nuance: வாசந்தி in line 1 is obscure; it rhymes with ஆசந்தி (bier) in line 3, setting the wedding against the funeral. பாசம் may be the bond of love that is burned with him or simply the body. The verse makes the wife's mourning a matter of form (அமைய அழுதிட்டு).

151.reading: The physician lets go the hand after feeling the pulse, the mind fails and the axle breaks, and the five who ate rice with ghee poured on it are gone; while the kohl-eyed wife and the wealth stay behind, this is how one takes leave and quits the body.
151.nuance: The five (ஐவர்) are traditionally the five senses, fed well and the first to leave; the same five return in 188. அச்சற (the axle breaking) is read of the body as a cart. What stays (wife, wealth) and what goes (the man) are set side by side.

152.reading: The pandal has come apart, the storehouse has lost its fastenings, all nine gates are shut together; as the time of pain brings defilement on and on, the loving ones wept and went away.
152.nuance: The nine gates (ஒன்பது வாசல்) are the body's nine openings, an image Tirumular uses again in 175. துரிசு (defilement, fault) may be the decay of the corpse.

153.reading: The lord of the land, the chief of our town, mounts for the last time a palanquin of the burning ground; with the people following behind and drums beating in front, this is how the land's lord walks.
153.nuance: Every mark of a royal procession is kept, the palanquin, the following crowd, the drums, but the palanquin is the bier (காட்டுச் சிவிகை). The verse lets the irony stand without comment.

154.reading: Thirty and thirty and thirty-six live in a temple with a well-built wall; once that walled temple fell to ruin, all of them alike ran off.
154.nuance: 30 + 30 + 36 makes ninety-six, the number of the body's constituents (tattvas) in a later Tamil count; that is how the verse is traditionally read, though it names no tattvas. The body is called a கோயில (temple) here, an idea Tirumular develops elsewhere.

155.reading: Leaving behind the woman with honeyed hair, the wealth and the house, he mounts the platform, and looking toward the common burning ground outside the town they lifted him, set him down and went away.
155.nuance: இதணம் (a raised platform) is taken as the bier. மதுவூர வாங்கியே in line 4 is obscure; it echoes மதுவூர் in line 1 and may be corrupt.

156.reading: Even seeing him set down and left, people think the rare wealth they seek will not leave them; those who chase it like madness grow weak without ever leaving off.
156.nuance: The first line takes up வைத்தகன்றார் from 155. Lines 3 and 4 (பிச்சது வாய்ப்பின் தொடர்வுறு மற்றவர் எச்சகலா) are obscure, and this reading of them is a guess.

157.reading: The kin who rise up wailing, the wives and the children, turn back at the edge of the town; after that they strip him, pile the wood and light the fire, then plunge headfirst into the water, people without justice.
157.nuance: நீதியிலோர் (those without justice) is a harsh last word for the mourners; it may mean only that they do what custom requires and no more. வேர்த்தலை போக்கி is unclear.

158.reading: Over the whole wide land the potter shaped pots from the tank's clay; when a pot breaks people keep the pieces as shards, but when the body breaks they will not keep it even a moment.
158.nuance: The broken pot is still worth something, the broken body nothing. Line 1 (வளத்திடை முற்றத்தோர்) is hard to construe.

159.reading: Five tufts, six braids, thirty joints, eighteen supports, nine pandals and fifteen rows: it lay burnt, and we know nothing beyond that.
159.nuance: The numbers describe the body as a built thing, but what each stands for is not given and I can't fix it; tradition matches them to the elements, senses and other parts. The plain point is the last line: all this lay burnt, and what came after is unknown.

160.reading: They chopped fig fruit and good spinach seed, put them in the pot and cooked a gruel; when the spinach seed ate the fig, those who held the knife went to the burning ground.
160.nuance: A riddle with no key in the verse. The fig and the seed are commonly taken as parts of the body, or as body and karma, and the gruel as the body's making; I can't fix the reference. Only the end, the cooks going to the burning ground, is plain.

161.reading: There is no ridge above and no eave below; there are two posts and one ridge beam; it is a silver dwelling thatched not by those who thatch with palm leaf but by a craftsman.
161.nuance: The two posts and one beam repeat 146. வேலையான் may be the craftsman who made the body, taken as the Lord, and வெள்ளித் தளிகை (silver dish or dwelling) is unclear. Line 3 (ஊடு வரியாமை) is hard to construe.

162.reading: The hall lies there but its adornments are gone; the dancing rhythm has ceased altogether; some sing and weep in tune, and they put it in the fire they gathered.
162.nuance: The hall (கூடம்) is the body; the ceased rhythm (இலயம்) may be breath or pulse. தீயவைத்தார் plays on தீ (fire) and தீய (the bad thing), so the corpse becomes something unclean to be burned.

163.reading: The egg was born in three hundred days, though nothing was put there, poor people; at twelve years it knew marriage, at seventy it perished, and you do not see the ruin.
163.nuance: The egg is the body, carried about three hundred days in the womb. இட்டது தானிலை ஏதேனும் is obscure: perhaps that no one can say who laid it. The verse compresses a whole life into three numbers.

164.reading: While the lamp bowl stays, he took away the flame; fools who don't know it is over cry aloud, and the world, not knowing that dawn turns to darkness, lies sunk and trembles.
164.nuance: The bowl is the body and the flame the life. The taker (கொண்டான்) is not named; Death or the Lord both fit. The mourners are called fools for weeping over the bowl.

165.reading: Those who do not worship the form of the one with spreading konrai blossoms, who made body and life, lie suffering in the seventh hell, where they cry out as their entrails burn.
165.nuance: The konrai wearer is Siva. மாயன் may be another epithet of him (the wondrous one) or name Vishnu as maker; and the line may mean not worshipping him who made body and life, or not worshipping him with body and life. ஏழா நரகு is read as the seventh, lowest hell.

166.reading: With umbrella, horse and victorious sword the time passed in between; when the man goes, at that moment the precious life reaches its place, left or right.
166.nuance: The umbrella, horse and sword are the signs of rule, the life between birth and death. இடம் வலம் (left, right) is commonly taken as the bad or good destination the life reaches according to its deeds; it may also mean only that it goes wherever it goes. Lines 2 and 3 are hard to construe.

167.reading: Once the dancer who stood in the skin bag, worked it to the end and fed it has left, what does it matter if crows carry off this nest, onlookers revile it, drops of milk are poured on it or many praise it?
167.nuance: The dancer (கூத்தன்) is the life that moved the body; a theological reading makes it the dancing Lord. பாற்றுளி (drops of milk) is the milk poured in the funeral rites, and பழிச்சில் means 'if they praise', answering பழிக்கில் (if they revile). The body is called கூடு, a nest or cage.

links.note: The two verses share most of their words: the dancer in the skin bag who worked it and has left, and the indifference of what is then done to the body. Tirumular lists crows, revilers, milk drops and praisers; the Naladiyar dragging, careful burial, casting out and revilers.
Both build the body as a hut with two posts and one ridge beam. 146 says the life can't re-enter once the roof comes apart; 161 adds that it was thatched by a maker, not by ordinary thatchers.
The Kural says the world's 'greatness' is that one who was here yesterday is gone today; Tirumular shows it in a single evening: a meal, a talk with his wife, a small ache, and he is gone.

Both tell a death as a short row of ordinary acts: the Naladiyar's 'he stood, he sat, he lay down, he went', Tirumular's cooking, eating, talking and lying down. The Naladiyar draws the lesson to do good now; Tirumular draws none.
The Kural calls virtue the companion that does not perish when one perishes; Tirumular says that when the body falls only vows and knowledge go on the road with the dead, not wife or children.

Both take a king to make the point: the Naladiyar's kings under moon-white umbrellas were carried off and called dead, Tirumular's lord of the land rides a bier with the town behind and drums in front.
Both make the body a clay pot. 143 has it melt back to clay in the rain; 158 says even a broken pot is kept as shards, but a broken body is not kept a moment.
145 ends the funeral with the bath that ends remembering; 157 retells it with the kin turning back at the town's edge and calls those who bathe and leave 'people without justice'.

143 compares dying people to the unfired vessel that turns back to clay when rain falls (விண்ணின்று நீர்விழின் மீண்டுமண் ணானார்ப்போல்). Kural 660 compares wealth got by deceit to water poured into a pot of wet clay (பசுமண் கலத்துள்நீர்). The unfired pot that water destroys stands for the body in 143 and for ill-gotten wealth in the Kural.

143 opens: from one clay, see, two kinds of vessel (மண்ணொன்று கண்டீர் இருவகைப் பாத்திரம்), and one of them returns to clay. 440 opens almost the same way, one clay becomes many good vessels (மண்ணொன்று தான்பல நற்கலமாயிடும்), to show the one Lord in all wombs. The same opening leads to the body's death in 143 and to the Lord's unity in 440.

144 says nothing goes along the road with the dead but the vows they kept and the knowledge they gained (கொண்ட விரதமும் ஞானமும் அல்லது). Naladiyar 120 says nothing goes with a person but the deeds they did (தாஞ்செய் வினையல்லால்), good or bad. Both strip away kin and body; Tirumular names only the good companions, the Naladiyar the deeds of either kind.

146 counts the body as a hut, two posts, one ridge beam and thirty-two rafters, so that its collapse is final. 594 counts it as a house with seven windows, two great doors, a cave and a bedchamber (எழுசாலேகம் இரண்டு பெருவாய்தல்) where the held breath can make one live long. The same counted house is shown falling in 146 and kept standing by breath in 594.

147 gives death's cause as the store of deeds running out (செய்வினை மூட்டிற்ற). Naladiyar 3 says even kings under the umbrella fall when their deeds are exhausted (வினைஉலப்ப வேறாகி வீழ்வர்). Both make the end come when the karma that held the life is spent.

149 shows the man who built a mansion in the square, rode a palanquin and gave away three crores, and did not turn back when called to go (சென்றத்தா என்னத் திரிந்திலன்). Thiruppugazh 1187 has the walled mansion and gold in the house (மாடமதிட் சுற்று ... கனக்க) until the body is tied to the bier and given to the fire. Both set public splendour directly against the bier.

156 says people, even seeing the dead man set down and left, think the wealth they seek will not leave them (அச்சகலாதென நாடும் அரும்பொருள்). Naladiyar 182 says fools think their household supports are secure and go heedless (பொச்சாந்து ஒழுகுவர் பேதையார்), though those supports only seem to stand. Both locate the folly in trusting what one has just seen fail.

158 has the potter shaping pots from the tank's clay; broken pots are kept as shards, but a broken body is not kept a moment (உடலுடைந்தால் இறைப்போதும் வையாரே). 443 has the potter shaping whatever is in his mind (குசவன் மனத்துற்ற தெல்லாம் வனைவன்), as Nandi shapes the world. The potter shows the Lord's making in 443 and the worthlessness of the made body in 158.

159 counts the body in riddling numbers, five tufts, six braids, thirty joints, eighteen supports, before it lies burnt. 2888 counts its tenants the same way, ten tigers, fifteen elephants, five skilled ones, sixteen entertainers (பத்துப் பரும்புலி யானை பதினைந்து). Both encode the tattvas of the body as a numbered riddle; 159 ends in the fire, 2888 in the assembly that sits within.

162 says the hall lies there but its adornments are gone and the dancing rhythm has ceased (ஆடும் இலயமும் அற்றது). 189 has a drum and two cymbals and a king within; when the king goes out the drum becomes clay (மத்தளி மண்ணாய்). Both make the living body a place of music that falls silent when the life leaves.

164 says the flame was taken while the lamp bowl remained (இடிஞ்சில் இருக்க விளக்கெரி கொண்டான்), and fools who do not know it is over cry out. 749 repeats the words (முடிந்தது அறியார் ... இடிஞ்சில் இருக்க விளக்கெரி கொண்டு) but turns them to yoga: those who can catch the flame may reach the goal while living. The near-repeat serves death in 164 and the yogi's practice in 749.

165 says those who do not worship the form of the one who made body and life lie in the seventh hell (ஏழா நரகிற் கிடப்பர்). 264 asks those who neither praise the Supreme nor give to beggars whether they will stand in hell (நரகத்தில் நிற்றிரோ). Both name failure to worship as the road to hell; 264 adds failure to give.

165 sets those who do not worship in the seventh hell, crying out as their entrails burn. Thiruppugazh 393 asks for Murugan's two feet so as not to enter the fire-mouthed hell (எரிவாய் நரகிற் புகுதாதபடிக்கு இருபாதம் எனக்கருள்வாயே). Tirumular's warning becomes Arunagiri's prayer.

166 says the time passed between with umbrella, horse and victorious sword (குடையும் குதிரையும் கொற்றவாளும்), and at death the life reaches its place, left or right. Naladiyar 3 has kings riding on elephants under the umbrella (குடைநிழற்கீழ்) who fall when their deeds run out. Both use the royal regalia to show that rank does not decide the end.

167 calls the body a nest (இக்கூட்டையே) the dancer has left, so what is done to it no longer matters. Kural 338 likens body and life to a bird flying off and leaving its nest alone (குடம்பை தனித்து ஒழியப் புள்பறந்தற்றே). Tirumular takes the Kural's empty nest and asks why anyone should care for it.

167 dismisses the nest the dancer has left (புறப்பட்டுப் போன இக்கூட்டையே). 2852 adds that if the nest perishes there is one who will make another (கூடு கெடின் மற்றோர் கூடுசெய் வான்உளன்), and that this is no loss to those who know Nandi. 2852 gives the reason for 167's indifference.

source_issues: 163 line 1 reads முந்_று, apparently a damaged முந்நூறு (three hundred); line 3 reads பன்னிரண்டி ஆண்டினில், probably for பன்னிரண்டாண்டினில்.
155 line 4 (மதுவூர வாங்கியே), 156 lines 3 and 4, 157 line 3 (வேர்த்தலை போக்கி) and 161 line 3 (ஊடு வரியாமை) are obscure and may be corrupt.
167 shares most of its wording with Naladiyar 26; which text borrowed is not settled here.
